title: Act IV, Scene III
focus: testing loyalty and the cost of grief

teacherSummary.text: In England, Malcolm tests Macduff by claiming to be lustful, greedy and without any of the 'king-becoming graces.' When Macduff despairs ('O Scotland, Scotland!'), Malcolm reveals it was a test and that old Siward with ten thousand men is ready. A Doctor describes King Edward healing the sick by touch. Ross arrives and, after hesitating, tells Macduff his wife and children have been slaughtered. Macduff asks 'All my pretty ones?' and, told to 'dispute it like a man,' answers 'I shall do so; but I must also feel it as a man.' He vows to face Macbeth.

context.history: The 'king's evil' (scrofula) was believed to be cured by a monarch's touch; James I continued the ceremony. The scene contrasts a healing king with a destroying one.

significance: The long test scene defines good kingship, and Macduff's grief redefines manhood: feeling is not weakness. This answers Lady Macbeth's use of manhood in I.vii.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior

writingPrompts.label: AP

Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of testing loyalty and the cost of grief responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of testing loyalty and the cost of grief follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene III and its treatment of testing loyalty and the cost of grief. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about testing loyalty and the cost of grief in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of testing loyalty and the cost of grief. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does it mean to 'be a man' or to be strong? Has the meaning changed? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: A father learns his family has been killed.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are transpose, hoodwink, rawness, demerits, whetstone. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “But I shall crave your pardon;
That which you are my thoughts cannot transpose:
Angels are bright still, though the brightest fell:
Though all things foul would wear the brows of grace,
Yet grace must still look so.” In this sentence it means: to change. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Macbeth would have known. The 'king's evil' (scrofula) was believed to be cured by a monarch's touch; James I continued the ceremony. The scene contrasts a healing king with a destroying one. Why does this scene matter? The long test scene defines good kingship, and Macduff's grief redefines manhood: feeling is not weakness. This answers Lady Macbeth's use of manhood in I.vii. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script:
Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “What I believe I’ll wail,
What know believe, and what I can redress,
As I shall find the time to friend, I will.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to testing loyalty and the cost of grief? I circle “blisters”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find characterization, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
